Surendra Singh.description: King of Naugarh and father of Virendra Singh; a wise and respected ruler who later resides in Chunar.

Virendra Singh.description: Son of Surendra Singh and King of Chunar. Husband of Chandrakanta, father of Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh. A just and powerful ruler waging war against Shivdutt.

Chandrakanta.description: Daughter of Maharaj Jay Singh of Vijaygarh; wife of Virendra Singh and mother of Indrajeet Singh and Anand Singh.

Maharaj Jay Singh.description: King of Vijaygarh and father of Chandrakanta.

Tej Singh.description: A prominent ayyār (spy/magician) known for his cunning; later becomes chief minister to Raja Virendra Singh.

Maharaj Shivdutt.description: King of Chunar and rival to Surendra Singh; known for his old grudges and villainy.

Chapla.description: Ayyara (female ayyār), married to Tej Singh; sister of Champa.

Champa.description: Ayyara, married to Devi Singh; sister of Chapla.

Fateh Singh.description: Entrusted with the throne of Naugarh when Surendra Singh moves to Chunar.

Jeet Singh.description: Ayyār and close confidant of Surendra Singh; becomes tutor and protector of the princes.

Indrajeet Singh.description: Elder son of Virendra Singh and Chandrakanta; skilled and adventurous prince, central to the story.

Anand Singh.description: Younger son of Virendra Singh and Chandrakanta; accompanies Indrajeet Singh on adventures.

Bhairon Singh.description: Son of Tej Singh and Chapla; a clever and skilled ayyār, close to Indrajeet Singh.

Tara Singh.description: Son of Devi Singh and Champa; a talented ayyār, close to Anand Singh.

Pannalal.description: An ayyār who, along with others, tests and trains Bhairon Singh and Tara Singh.

Kanchan Singh.description: Commander of the army accompanying the princes on their hunting expedition.

Babaji.description: A mysterious sadhu (holy man) who rides lions and is later revealed to be an ayyār in disguise.

Bawaji.description: Alternate spelling of Babaji, used in dialogue; the same character.

Gandhakarta.description: A character who appears with Shivdutt at the end of the chapter, likely an associate or henchman.

Naugarh.description: A kingdom ruled by Surendra Singh, later entrusted to Fateh Singh.

Vijaygarh.description: A kingdom ruled by Maharaj Jay Singh, father of Chandrakanta.

Chunar.description: A kingdom formerly ruled by Shivdutt, later the seat of Virendra Singh's rule and the main setting.

Girnar.description: A place mentioned by Babaji as his destination, known in India as a sacred mountain.

Raja.description: A royal title meaning 'king' or 'prince' in Hindi.

Maharaj.description: A royal title meaning 'great king' in Hindi.

banrakhas.description: Forest guards or keepers responsible for assisting in hunts.

dhuni.description: A sacred fire kept by ascetics or sadhus for meditation and rituals.

Kshatriya.description: A member of the warrior and ruler caste in traditional Hindu society.

Brahma.description: The Hindu god of creation, referenced here as a symbol of supreme authority.

aiyyar.description: A master of disguise, espionage, and trickery; a spy or magician in the context of the novel.

tilism.description: A magical realm, labyrinth, or enchanted puzzle that must be solved or broken.

babaji.description: A term of respect for a holy man or ascetic.

sadhu.description: A Hindu holy man or ascetic, often depicted as wandering and spiritually advanced.

mahātma.description: A great soul; a term of respect for a spiritually advanced person or saint.

ayyaars.description: Plural of aiyyar; refers to the group of spies/magicians in the story.

kos.description: An ancient Indian unit of distance, approximately 2-3 kilometers.

Kunwar Virendra Singh.description: A prince and rival of Maharaj Shivdutt, victorious in their conflict.

King Chet Singh.description: A famous king of Kashi, formerly associated with the ancient ruined fort near Ahraura.

Nazim.description: A Muslim ayyar, mentioned as a possible relative of the three ayyars serving Shivdutt.

Ahmad.description: A Muslim ayyar, also mentioned as a possible relative of the three ayyars serving Shivdutt.

Bakar Ali.description: One of the three chief Muslim ayyars in Shivdutt's service, skilled in espionage and disguise.

Khudabakhsh.description: One of the three chief Muslim ayyars serving Maharaj Shivdutt.

Yar Ali.description: One of the three chief Muslim ayyars serving Maharaj Shivdutt.

Indrajit Singh.description: The elder son of Raja Virendra Singh and Chandrakanta, a brave and handsome prince (Kunwar). He is the central hero of the story, skilled in warfare and deeply in love with Kishori.

Vindhya.description: A mountain range in central India, whose forests serve as the setting for Shivdutt's retreat.

Robertsganj.description: A town in Uttar Pradesh, India, mentioned as part of the forest region.

Sarguja.description: A region in central India, included in the stretch of the Vindhya forest.

Singrauli.description: A district in central India, also part of the forested area described.

Ahraura.description: A town near Chunar, noted for its ancient ruined fort.

Kashi.description: The ancient name for Varanasi, a major city in India associated with King Chet Singh.

Shivduttgarh.description: The name given by Shivdutt to the old fort where he takes refuge and establishes his base.

Bhil.description: An indigenous tribal community of central India, among the hill tribes led by Shivdutt.

Kharwar.description: Another indigenous tribal group of central India, also led by Shivdutt.

Kunwar.description: A title meaning 'prince' or 'young nobleman' in Hindi.

ayyari.description: The art or craft of being an aiyyar, involving disguise, intelligence gathering, and trickery.

garh.description: A Hindi word meaning 'fort' or 'fortress', often used as a suffix in place names.

Maharaj Surendra Singh.description: The king of Chunar Fort and grandfather to Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh; a wise and respected ruler.

Bhairon.description: An aiyyār who disguised himself as Indrajit Singh and allowed himself to be captured by Shivdutt's spies.

Shivdutt.description: A rival king or prince, antagonist to the Chunar royals, known for employing cunning ayyars.

Ramnarayan.description: Another aiyyār or agent sent to help Bhairon Singh.

Chunnilal.description: Another aiyyār or agent sent to help Bhairon Singh.

Badrinath.description: An aiyyār or agent, notable for his swimming prowess and involvement in aiding Bhairon Singh.

Jyotishiji.description: An aiyyār or advisor, possibly with astrological expertise, sent to assist Bhairon Singh.

Chamberlain.description: A senior servant or official in the royal household, responsible for relaying messages and managing guests.

Attendant.description: A servant who announces visitors and assists the princes.

Chunar Fort.description: A historic fort and the seat of the Chunar royal family, serving as the main setting for much of the story.

Shivdutt's ayyars.description: The group of spies and magicians employed by Shivdutt.

Shivdattgarh.description: A fortress or city under Shivdutt's control.

Ganga.description: The sacred river Ganges, central to many scenes in the chapter.

barahdari.description: A pavilion with twelve doors, common in Mughal and Indian architecture, often used for gatherings.

mridang.description: A traditional Indian percussion instrument, similar to a drum.

siddha.description: A spiritually perfected or enlightened person, often with supernatural powers.

Kunwar Anand Singh.description: Another young prince who also goes missing alongside Indrajit Singh.

Jeetsingh.description: A trusted advisor and possibly an aiyyar, who helps strategize and coordinate the search efforts.

Tejsingh.description: A loyal and resourceful aide, likely an aiyyar, who leads the search party and coordinates military action.

Devisingh.description: Another trusted associate summoned for counsel regarding the disappearance.

Shivdatt.description: An antagonist whose resurgence is suspected to be behind the recent troubles.

Dev Singh.description: A member of the royal circle who is consulted about the mysterious corpse.

Tarasingh.description: A character considered for a mission to Badrinath to assist Bhaironsingh.

Bhaironsingh.description: A character mentioned as needing to be freed, possibly an ally in trouble.

turret.description: A small tower on top of a fort or castle, often used for lookout or signaling.

kettledrum.description: A large drum used in Indian courts and armies for signaling or ceremonial purposes.

mallet.description: A hammer-like tool used to strike the kettledrum.

audience hall.description: A formal hall in a palace where the king meets with courtiers and the public.

torchbearers.description: Individuals who carry torches, especially in processions or at night for illumination.

Pandit Badrinath.description: A skilled aiyyar and leader of the rescue party, known for his intelligence and resourcefulness.

Jagannath Jyotishi.description: Also referred to as Jyotishiji, he is a learned astrologer and aiyyar who aids in the rescue mission.

Bhaironsingh Aiyar.description: A brave and resourceful aiyyar who is initially imprisoned in Shivdattgarh but later escapes.

Kanchansingh.description: Commander who oversees the search for the lion-clad Babaji and Bhaironsingh.

Baqar Ali Ayyar.description: The old jailor and aiyyar who cleverly traps Ramnarayan and Chunnilal, later rewarded for his cunning.

Aiyar.description: A term for a master spy, disguise artist, and magician in the world of Chandrakanta.

Aiyars.description: Plural of 'Aiyar', referring to the group of skilled spies and magicians.

Jyotishi.description: A term for an astrologer; in this context, refers to Jagannath Jyotishi.

Halwai.description: A sweet-seller or confectioner, commonly found in Indian towns and villages.

ayyars.description: Plural of 'aiyyar', referring to a group of such agents.

peda.description: A type of Indian sweet made from condensed milk and sugar, often flavored with cardamom.

puri.description: A deep-fried, unleavened Indian bread, commonly eaten with various accompaniments.

seer.description: A traditional Indian unit of weight, roughly equivalent to about 0.93 kilograms or 2 pounds.

anna.description: A former Indian currency unit, equal to 1/16 of a rupee.

Ajay Singh.description: A cunning character who betrays the ayyars, aiding their capture.

Chanla.description: A female companion or attendant of Chandrakanta, often involved in her adventures.

halwai.description: A confectioner or sweet-maker in Indian culture.

Soldier.description: A mysterious, resourceful man who helps Anand Singh escape captivity, refusing to reveal his true identity.

Woman.description: A beautiful, enigmatic woman who imprisons Anand Singh and tries to win his love, later revealed to possess magical or supernatural abilities.

Abyssinian girl.description: A young, beautiful attendant of the main woman, holding a dagger and assisting in the torture scene.

Abyssinian man.description: An ugly attendant who assists the main woman by digging in the pit.

Yogini.description: A formidable female ascetic with supernatural powers, who intervenes at the end of the chapter, rendering everyone unconscious with her magic.

Falak-e-Haftum.description: The seventh and highest level of heaven in Islamic cosmology, referenced as a mark of honor.

Khuda.description: An Urdu/Persian word for God, commonly used by Muslims.

Ram-Ram.description: A traditional Hindu greeting or exclamation invoking the deity Rama.

Abyssinian.description: Refers to people of Ethiopian origin; in Indian literature, often denotes African slaves or attendants.

nimcha.description: A type of curved sword, originally from North Africa but used in India as well.

lota.description: A small, rounded metal vessel used for storing and pouring liquids, especially water or milk.

yogini.description: A female ascetic or practitioner of yoga, often depicted as possessing mystical powers in Indian tradition.

pishachi.description: A female demon or evil spirit in Hindu mythology, often associated with vampiric or ghostly traits.

betel box.description: A container for storing betel leaves and accompaniments, used in the preparation of paan (a traditional Indian chew).

tripund.description: Three horizontal lines of sacred ash worn on the forehead by Shaivite Hindus.

veranda.description: A roofed, open-air gallery or porch attached to a house, common in Indian architecture.

maidservant.description: A female domestic worker or attendant, often serving noblewomen in Indian households.

skull-cup.description: A ritual vessel made from a human skull, used in Tantric and ascetic practices in India.

ash.description: Sacred ash (vibhuti) used by Hindu ascetics for ritual purposes, often smeared on the body.

Bhimsen.description: Bhimsen is the eighteen-year-old son of Maharaj Shivdatt, known for his physical strength, skills in weaponry, and fondness for hunting.

Kishori.description: Kishori is the fifteen-year-old daughter of Maharaj Shivdatt, currently sent away to her maternal grandparents' home due to her father's displeasure.

Bakr Ali.description: An ayyaar (spy/agent) serving Maharaj Shivdutt, tasked with releasing Virendra Singh's ayyaars and returning their belongings.

Shivdatt Singh.description: Another name for Maharaj Shivdutt, used interchangeably in the text.

Miyan Bakar.description: Another name for Bakr Ali, used by the ayyaars in a familiar or teasing way.

Bhim.description: Shortened form of Bhimsen, used in his letter and by others.

Raja Sahib.description: A respectful term for a king or ruler, likely referring to Shivdutt in this context.

Kumar Bhimsen.description: A formal title for Prince Bhimsen, indicating his royal status.

Prince Virendra Singh.description: Alternate title for Raja Virendra Singh, emphasizing his royal lineage.

ayyārs.description: Plural form of ayyaar, referring to the group of spies/magicians.

muddu.description: A tilism term, possibly meaning a magical being or person of interest, as noted in the text.

chobdar.description: A ceremonial usher or attendant, often responsible for delivering messages in royal courts.

masha.description: A traditional Indian unit of weight, often used for gold or precious materials.

howdah.description: A seat or carriage mounted on the back of an elephant, used for riding.

palanquins.description: Covered litters carried by bearers, used for transporting people, especially nobility.

Miyan.description: A respectful or familiar address, often used for Muslim men.

daggers.description: Short, pointed knives, commonly carried by warriors and spies in the story.

Vanchari.description: A provisional name given to the second woman accompanying the Yogini, whose true identity is yet to be disclosed.

Habshi.description: A person involved in the events of the cave, responsible for digging a grave and assisting the Yogini and others.

sari.description: A traditional Indian garment worn by women, consisting of a long piece of cloth draped around the body.

jalchari.description: A Hindi term meaning 'water nymph' or 'water-dweller', used here to describe the young woman emerging from the pond.

Kamla.description: An ayyar (spy/magician) who is Kishori's devoted companion, skilled in disguise and espionage, and determined to help Kishori reunite with Indrajit Singh.

Madhavi.description: A woman skilled in disguise, who deceives others by taking on Kishori's appearance and is implicated in the abduction of Indrajit Singh.

Vaikunth.description: In Hindu cosmology, the celestial abode of Lord Vishnu; here it is used metaphorically to mean 'sent to the afterlife' or 'killed.'

Pari Jamal.description: Mentioned in Kishori's letter as the woman who has deceived Indrajit Singh by making herself look like Kishori.

Santati.description: Refers to the four parts or volumes of the story, possibly meaning 'descendants' or 'generations' in Hindi.

haveli.description: A traditional Indian mansion or large house, often grand and ornate.

stepwell.description: A well or water storage structure in which the water is reached by descending a set of steps, common in India.

maiden.description: An archaic term for a young, unmarried woman.

portrait.description: A painted or drawn representation of a person, often used in the story as a token of identity or love.

tunnel.description: A passageway, often underground, used here to refer to a secret or hidden route.

canal.description: A man-made waterway, but in this context, it may refer to a natural or artificial water channel or cave.

Lalita.description: One of Madhavi's two closest companions, Lalita is skilled in the art of ayyari and is trusted by Madhavi.

Tilottama.description: Madhavi's other close companion, Tilottama is also an expert in ayyari and provides counsel to Madhavi.

Chandaal.description: A powerful figure who holds sway over the affairs of the state in Gayaji, feared by Madhavi for his potential to ruin everything.

Gayaji.description: A region or kingdom where Madhavi rules, and the setting for much of the intrigue in this chapter.

dark woman.description: A mysterious, clever woman who aids Indrajit Singh with her cunning and resourcefulness, orchestrating secret plans and facilitating his movements.

Diwan.description: The middle-aged man seen with Madhavi; he is her chief minister or administrator, wielding significant influence within the kingdom.

Kalavati.description: Sister of Mayavati and wife of Shivdutt, Kalavati is Kishori's mother.

Mayavati.description: Sister of Kalavati, wife of Chandraddatt, and mother of Madhavi.

Chandraddatt.description: King of Gaya, husband of Mayavati, and father of Madhavi, known for his indulgent lifestyle.

Agnidatt.description: The minister of the kingdom, one of the three chief men holding real power.

Kuver Singh.description: The commander of the kingdom's forces, one of the three chief men.

Dharam Singh.description: The city's chief constable, one of the three chief men in the kingdom.

Kumar Indrajit Singh.description: A prince who is currently lying helpless in Rajgriha.

Chachi.description: A character referenced as someone who might ensnare Lalita and Tilottama.

Gaya.description: A city and kingdom ruled by Chandraddatt, also a famous pilgrimage site in India.

Rajgriha.description: A hill and pilgrimage site near Gaya where Chandraddatt built a mansion and spent much of his time.

Diwan Sahib.description: A formal title referring to the minister or chief administrator.

Senapati.description: A title meaning commander or general of the army.

Kotwal.description: A title for the chief constable or head of city police.

vanchari.description: A wandering woman or female ascetic, often associated with forests or rural areas.

Diwan Agniddatt.description: A diwan (minister or high official) allied with Madhavi, involved in the intrigues against Indrajit Singh.

Maharaj Virendra Singh.description: The powerful ruler of Chunar, respected and feared, under whose protection Kishori would be safe.

Maharani Chandrakanta.description: The queen of Chunar, she supports Kishori and sends Kamla to bring her to Chunar, showing her approval of Kishori.

Ram.description: A revered deity in Hinduism, invoked here as a protector in a moment of uncertainty.

Nagauri.description: Refers to a breed of oxen from Nagaur, Rajasthan, known for their strength and speed, used to draw the chariot.

Maharani.description: A royal title meaning 'queen,' used for female rulers such as Chandrakanta.

watch.description: A traditional Indian unit of time, roughly equivalent to about three hours, used to divide the night.

chariot.description: A horse- or oxen-drawn carriage, often used for travel by nobility or royalty.

orchard.description: A garden or plantation of fruit trees, here specifically a mango orchard.

maidservants.description: Female domestic workers or attendants, commonly found in royal or noble households.

waning moon.description: The phase of the moon when it is decreasing in illumination, often used in Indian literature to mark time or atmosphere.

Manraj.description: A figure mentioned as love-intoxicated, whose command guides the movement of prayer beads; likely a devotee or spiritual figure.

Girijapati.description: A divine name invoked during prayers, referring to Lord Shiva, the consort of Goddess Parvati (Girija).

Jahnavi.description: A divine name for the river Ganga, personified as a goddess whose waters are believed to cleanse sins.

King Virendrasingh.description: The ruler of a kingdom, he is one of the two men on the hill, depicted as a person of high standing and authority.

Prince Anandasingh.description: The younger son of King Virendrasingh, a brave young man around twenty years old, standing with his father and Tejsingh.

Bahadur.description: A brave soldier who descends the hill to rejoin the army; 'Bahadur' is also a common title or honorific for a courageous man.

sal.description: A type of tree (Shorea robusta) native to the Indian subcontinent, often found in forests.

shisham.description: Also known as Indian rosewood (Dalbergia sissoo), a valuable hardwood tree common in India.

dhotis.description: Traditional Indian garments for men, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs.

rosary.description: A string of prayer beads used in Hindu (and other) devotional practices to count recitations of prayers or mantras.

anointing.description: The ritual act of applying oil, ash, or sandalwood paste to the body, often as part of religious observance.

garland-maker.description: A person who makes garlands, typically of flowers, for religious offerings or adornment.

pendant.description: An ornament that hangs from jewelry, such as earrings or necklaces; in this context, a flower used in place of a traditional pendant.

Diwan Agnidatt.description: The chief minister (Diwan) of Madhavi's court, favored by Madhavi and close friends with Kuber Singh and Dharm Singh.

Kuber Singh.description: The commander (Senapati) of Madhavi's forces and one of the three chief men at her court.

Dharm Singh.description: The kotwal (chief of police) of Madhavi's realm and one of the three chief men at her court.

Senapati Sahib.description: Honorific form of Kuber Singh, used throughout the chapter.

Kotwal Sahib.description: Honorific form of Dharm Singh, used throughout the chapter.

First Man.description: One of two young brothers from Gayaji who appear before the Kotwal with a dispute over a woman.

Second Man.description: The other young brother from Gayaji, also involved in the dispute over the mysterious woman.

First Brother.description: Refers to the First Man when guiding the Kotwal to the woman.

Second Brother.description: Refers to the Second Man when guiding the Kotwal to the woman.

Rani Madhavi.description: Another form of Madhavi's name, with 'Rani' meaning queen, confirming her royal status.

Madhavi's court.description: The royal court or palace where Queen Madhavi rules and her chief officials convene.

Rani.description: A Hindi word meaning 'queen', used as a title for royal women.

kotwal.description: The chief of police or head of city security in an Indian town or city.

sahib.description: An honorific term of respect, equivalent to 'sir' or 'lord'.

palanquin.description: A covered litter for one passenger, carried on poles by bearers, used in South Asia.

orderlies.description: Attendants or assistants, often soldiers serving a superior officer.

Randheersingh.description: Kishori's maternal grandfather, a powerful landlord who becomes enraged at Madhavi's actions.

Harnamsingh.description: Kamla's elder brother, who assists her in the search for Kishori.

Rewa.description: A place name; a region or kingdom through which one of the roads at the crossroads passes.

Garyaji.description: A place name; a destination reached by taking the road through Rewa.

ayyara.description: A female spy, trickster, or magician skilled in disguise and subterfuge.

diwan.description: A high-ranking official or chief minister in a royal court, responsible for administration.

Bhairav Singh.description: One of the protagonists, an ally working to rescue Indrajit Singh.

Jat.description: A specific location or object in the pond, possibly a platform or marker.

ayyaar.description: A master of disguise, espionage, and trickery; a spy or rogue with magical abilities.

Kunwar Indrajitsingh.description: A prince and the main protagonist, known for his bravery and determination; he is in love with Kishori and seeks to rescue her.

water tunnel.description: A secret passage previously used for movement within the palace, now sealed and replaced by another tunnel.

palace.description: The royal residence where much of the intrigue and action takes place.

underground chamber.description: A hidden room beneath the palace, accessible via secret tunnels.

cave.description: A subterranean area near the palace, possibly part of the tunnel system.

garden.description: A walled area surrounding the mansion, heavily guarded and central to the escape attempt.

mansion.description: A grand residence, here referring to the home of Madhavi's minister, Agnidatt.

Ayyars.description: A group of skilled spies, warriors, and masters of disguise, loyal to Indrajitsingh.

chandalini.description: A term referring to a cruel or merciless woman, derived from 'chandal', a member of a low caste associated with harshness.

Agniddatt.description: Also referred to as Diwan Sahib or Diwan Agnidatt, he is a villainous minister who abducts Kishori and schemes to seize the throne.

Kamini.description: The unmarried daughter of Agnidatt, she is of Kishori's age and is described as beautiful and good-natured.

Agnidatt's wife.description: The wife of Agnidatt, described as good-natured but suffering under her husband's cruelty.

Dussehra.description: Also known as Vijayadashami, a major Hindu festival celebrating the victory of good over evil.

Vijayadashami.description: Another name for Dussehra, marking the end of the Navaratri festival and the triumph of Lord Rama over Ravana.

Yama.description: The Hindu god of death, whose abode is referenced as a metaphor for being killed.

cavern.description: A large underground chamber, often used in the novel as a secret prison or hideout.

palace guards.description: Soldiers responsible for the security of the palace.

chief constable.description: The head of the city police or law enforcement, referred to as the kotwal in Hindi.

abode of Yama.description: A phrase meaning death or the afterlife, referencing the Hindu god of death.

Chandradhar.description: The former ruler or dynasty of Gaya, whose palace is now occupied by Virendra Singh's family.

Puranas.description: Ancient Hindu scriptures and mythological texts, referenced as a source of Anand Singh's knowledge.

Yamlok.description: In Hindu belief, the abode of Yama, the god of death; used metaphorically here to mean death or the afterlife.

Rambha.description: A celestial nymph (apsara) from Hindu mythology, symbolizing beauty.

Urvashi.description: Another famous apsara (celestial nymph) from Hindu mythology, renowned for her beauty.

vaidya.description: A traditional physician or healer, trained in Indian medicine.

petition chest.description: A locked box placed for subjects to submit written petitions or grievances to the ruler.

proclamation.description: An official public announcement, often regarding new laws or royal decisions.

candelabrum.description: A large branched candlestick holder, used for lighting rooms.

landlord.description: A person who owns large tracts of land, often with significant local influence.

noble.description: A person of high birth or aristocratic rank, often holding titles and land.

Ramshila.description: A hill near Gayaji, serving as the location where Dev Singh posts his note and observes the villains.

dacoit.description: A bandit or member of a gang of robbers, especially one operating in rural India.

bouquet.description: A bunch of flowers, often used here to refer to floral arrangements left as clues or tokens.

grotto.description: A small cave or cavern, used here as a hiding place for observation.

chamber.description: A private room, often used in palaces or large houses, sometimes with secret or special significance in the story.

Devsingh.description: An ayyār (spy/agent) who enters the chamber and discovers evidence of the violent struggle.

Kinnari.description: The name given by the narrator to the mysterious woman at the center of the intrigue, whose true identity is yet to be revealed.

ayyār.description: A term for a spy, trickster, or agent skilled in disguise, subterfuge, and sometimes magic, common in Indian fantasy literature.

Maharaja.description: A Sanskrit title meaning 'great king,' used for rulers of Indian princely states.

dacoits.description: Bandits or armed robbers, particularly those operating in rural India.

crier.description: An official who makes public announcements, often by shouting proclamations in public spaces.

sun god.description: Refers to Surya, the Hindu deity representing the sun, often invoked in poetic descriptions of sunrise or sunset.

dharma.description: A key concept in Indian philosophy and religion, meaning duty, righteousness, or moral law.

watches.description: Traditional divisions of the night in Indian timekeeping, each 'watch' representing a specific period.

Vishnu-Paduka.description: A significant religious site in Gaya, believed to be associated with the footprints of Lord Vishnu.

Falgu.description: A river that flows through Gaya, considered sacred and featuring prominently in the local geography.

guru.description: A spiritual teacher or guide, especially in Hinduism.

ber.description: A type of wild Indian jujube tree, known for its small edible fruit.

makoiche.description: A wild plant or tree, likely referring to a local species found in India.

dhau.description: A type of wild tree native to India, often found in forests and wastelands.

Devisinghji.description: The suffix 'ji' is an honorific used in Hindi to show respect.

Indrajitsingh.description: Indrajitsingh is an alternate spelling of Indrajit Singh, used in dialogue and narrative.

Anandsingh.description: Anandsingh is an alternate spelling of Anand Singh, used in dialogue and narrative.

Rajgrih.description: Rajgrih is an alternate spelling of Rajgriha, referring to the same city or estate.

sardar.description: Sardar is a title for a military or group leader, often used for commanders or chiefs in Indian contexts.

sardars.description: Sardars are leaders or commanders, especially of military units or groups.

estate.description: In this context, 'estate' refers to a large area of land or a domain under the control of a ruler or noble, often with administrative or strategic significance.

King Surendrasingh.description: A king and authority figure who, along with others, has issued strict orders regarding the treatment of ayyārs.

Virendrasingh.description: Another royal, likely related to Indrajitsingh, who has also given orders about ayyār protocol.

Vishnupaduka temple.description: A temple in the city, serving as a landmark near the house where Kamla leads Indrajitsingh.

pleasure garden.description: A type of ornamental garden designed for leisure and enjoyment, often found in royal or noble residences in India.

Phalgu River.description: A river, likely inspired by the real Phalgu River in Bihar, India, serving as a setting for Babaji's abode.

verandah.description: A roofed, open-air porch or gallery attached to a building, common in Indian architecture.

Naharsingh.description: A formidable and honorable warrior in Shivdutt's service, known for his vow to serve whoever defeats him in single combat.

Diwan Agnidutt.description: A minister or high-ranking official who captured Kishori.

Sadhu.description: A holy man or ascetic who intervenes to save Kishori and displays remarkable strength and skill.

Chief.description: The leader of a group who rescues Kishori's body from her captors in the mountain pass.

Phalgu.description: A river near Ramshila hill, significant for its association with the sadhu's dwelling.

Akhadnath Babaji.description: A mysterious holy man (Babaji) living on a mound in the Phalgu, known for saving Kishori's life; later revealed to be Dev Singh in disguise.

Prince Kalyan Singh.description: The prince of Rohtasgarh, target of a kidnapping plot to prevent Kishori's forced marriage.

Maharaj Kumar.description: The prince of Rohtasgarh, also referred to as Kalyan Singh, who performs daily rituals at the Shiva temple.

Mathuria Chaubes.description: A guise adopted by Badrinath and Bhaironsingh as Brahmin priests to infiltrate Rohtasgarh.

Rohtasgarh.description: A famous mountain fortress in Bihar, central to the plot as the site of Kishori's captivity and the focus of military action.

Rohitashm.description: The ancient name for Rohtasgarh, as referenced in historical accounts.

Son River.description: A major river in eastern India, near which Rohtasgarh is located.

Akbar.description: The Mughal emperor, mentioned in historical context regarding Rohtasgarh's antiquity.

Bihar.description: An Indian region where much of the novel's action takes place.

Shiva.description: A principal Hindu deity; temples dedicated to Shiva are significant settings in the chapter.

Yamuna.description: A sacred river and goddess in Hinduism; invoked in greetings by the disguised characters.

Mahatma.description: A term for a great or holy person, used here for a revered figure at the mountain's foot.

Jaan Jahanuma.description: A book by Raja Shivprasad Sitare-Hind, cited for historical information about Rohtasgarh.

Raja Shivprasad Sitare-Hind.description: An author and historian whose work is referenced for factual background.

prasad.description: A religious offering, usually food or flowers, given as a blessing after worship.

hom.description: A Vedic fire ritual involving offerings to the sacred fire.

bhang.description: An intoxicating drink made from cannabis leaves, traditionally consumed in some Indian rituals and festivals.

Chaube.description: A Brahmin subcaste, often serving as priests; here, a disguise used by the protagonists.

Chaubeyji.description: An honorific for a Chaube, used as a respectful address.

bazaar.description: A marketplace or commercial area, common in Indian towns and cities.

pranayama.description: A yogic practice of breath control, often performed during Hindu rituals.

Kalyan Singh.description: A prince whose abduction by ayyars is a turning point in the chapter.

Lali.description: A beautiful woman tasked with entertaining and watching over Kishori; she intervenes to protect Kishori from Kundan and reveals her authority over Kundan.

Kundan.description: A young noblewoman, initially appearing distressed and seeking escape, later revealed to have some authority and a hidden agenda; she is confronted by Lali.

kingdom.description: Refers to the royal domain or realm in which the events are taking place, indicating a setting of rival courts and intrigue.

Jagannath.description: The astrologer in Virendra Singh's camp, likely consulted for auspicious timings.

Digvijay Singh.description: King of the opposing side, holding Rohtasgarh and sending a letter to Virendra Singh.

Kunwar Kalyan Singh.description: The son of Digvijay Singh, now a prisoner of Virendra Singh.

munshi.description: A secretary, clerk, or scribe, often responsible for reading or writing letters.

standard.description: A military flag or banner, used here to signify the size of the army.

King Virendra Singh.description: The ruler whose camp is being guarded; he is a central royal figure in the story.

Fatehsingh.description: A loyal soldier who keeps watch over King Virendra Singh's tent.

Prince Indrajit Singh.description: Also called Kunwar Indrajit Singh or Kumar; the prince who is abducted and later rescued in this chapter.

Kishoriji.description: A person from Rohtasgarh who sends a message to Prince Indrajit Singh; likely a woman of importance.

Coachman.description: The driver of the chariot used to abduct Prince Indrajit Singh; he is killed during the escape.

Rider.description: A masked individual who rescues Prince Indrajit Singh from his abductors; later revealed to be a woman.

Kashmiri.description: Relating to Kashmir, a region in northern India; the cloak worn by the mysterious man is described as Kashmiri.

Narangi.description: A mysterious object or code word central to the intrigue, possibly connected to threats or magical elements.

Dadi.description: An old woman, referred to as 'old Dadi', who recognizes the special chest and provides guidance to Lali and Kishori.

baradari.description: A type of pavilion or building with twelve doors, common in Mughal and Indian architecture, often used for gatherings or as a passageway.

cubits.description: An ancient unit of length, roughly the length of a forearm, used here to describe the height of the wall.

Tara.description: The signatory of the note found by the prince; she is acting as a servant or agent and reports on the progress of their plans.

dhoti.description: A traditional Indian garment for men, consisting of a long piece of cloth wrapped around the waist and legs.

Sher Singh.description: An older, valorous man, Kamla's uncle and an experienced Aiyyar, formerly loyal to the king of Rohtasgarh.

Randhir Singh.description: Kishori's grandfather, once a friend of Digvijay Singh and associated with Sher Singh's family.

Ajayabghar.description: A mysterious and dangerous building, referred to as a 'house of wonders,' built in the middle of a pond and associated with strange tales and a witch.

mirzai.description: A traditional close-fitting jacket or tunic worn by men in India.

tendu.description: A tree (Diospyros melanoxylon) whose leaves are used for rolling bidis (Indian cigarettes).

asan.description: A tree (Terminalia alata) native to India, known for its durable wood.

salai.description: A tree (Boswellia serrata) native to India, known for producing frankincense.

jujube.description: A small, thorny tree (Ziziphus mauritiana) producing edible fruit, common in India.

executioner.description: A person appointed to carry out death sentences, often by beheading.

throne.description: A ceremonial chair for a ruler or deity, symbolizing authority and power.

Manji.description: Mentioned as 'old Manji,' this character is referenced as someone who had knowledge about the mysterious voice in the tunnel, though Lali claims Manji never told her anything about it.

House of Wonders.description: A mysterious and magical building within the fort, also referred to as the 'chamber of wonders,' containing secret passages and hidden dangers.

Raja Digvijay Singh.description: The ruler of Rohtasgarh fort and a rival to Virendra Singh; he is suspicious and cautious.

Ramanand.description: One of the two main ayyars serving Maharaj Digvijay Singh; trusted and witty, but attached to his beard.

Govindsingh.description: A highly skilled ayyar serving Maharaj Digvijay Singh, currently away on a mission to Chunar.

Daroga.description: The jailor or chief warden of the underground cells in Rohtasgarh, responsible for prisoners.

Shiva temple.description: A temple dedicated to the Hindu god Shiva, significant for previous ayyari and the capture of Kunwar Kalyan Singh.

adda.description: A local establishment or shop where people gather to drink hemp (ganja) and socialize.

dharmashala.description: A rest house or inn, often for travelers or pilgrims, where Tej Singh rents a room.

ayyar.description: A master of disguise, espionage, and trickery; a spy or magician in the context of the novel.

fakir.description: A wandering ascetic or holy man, often living on alms.

sanyasi.description: A Hindu renunciant who has given up worldly life for spiritual pursuits.

Brahmin.description: A member of the priestly caste in Hindu society.

vairagi.description: A type of ascetic or renunciant, often detached from worldly affairs.

ganja.description: A preparation of cannabis, commonly smoked or consumed for its intoxicating effects.

Pandit Badri Nath.description: An experienced and clever ayyar, trusted by Tej Singh to remain at the camp due to his skills.

Jyotishi Ji.description: One of the ayyars accompanying Tej Singh on his mission, later disguised as the Daroga.

Digvijaysingh.description: A maharaj (king) who controls the underground vault and is involved in the secret affairs of Rohtasgarh.

Daroga's book.description: A journal or record kept by the Daroga, containing daily happenings and secrets of the vault.

vault.description: The secret underground chamber in Rohtasgarh, containing treasures and guarded secrets.

mantras.description: Sacred chants or formulas, referenced here to emphasize the secrecy of the vault's affairs.

Pandit.description: A learned scholar, often with expertise in religious or scholarly matters.

watch of the night.description: A traditional way of dividing the night into segments for keeping time or guard duty.

Diwan Ramanandji.description: A title referring to Ramanand in his official capacity as a minister or high-ranking official.

Ramanandji.description: An honorific form of Ramanand, indicating respect or official status.

dungeon.description: An underground prison or chamber, often used for holding important captives.

executioners.description: Individuals responsible for carrying out executions or burials, often serving the king.

stupefaction.description: A state of being stunned or rendered unconscious, often by drugs or magical means.

Daroga Sahib.description: The title used for Jyotishiji in his official capacity as the jailor or chief of police in the dungeon.

Bhootnath.description: A fearsome black stone idol to whom sacrifices are made in the underground chamber, as per the established rules.

daroga.description: A Hindi/Urdu term for a police chief, jailor, or head of security.

ghadi.description: A traditional Indian unit of time, roughly equivalent to 24 minutes.

elixir.description: A medicinal or magical liquid, often used for healing or reviving characters.

Nanakprasad.description: A loyal and devoted man who accompanies Rambholi, assisting her in her secretive tasks and expressing deep love for her.

Rambholi.description: A mute and deaf young woman, skilled in disguise and action, who is on a mysterious mission involving secret objects and letters.

Nanak.description: An abbreviated form of Nanakprasad, used interchangeably in the text for the same character.

Koopdev.description: A mysterious entity associated with the well, who responds to the woman's call by offering water in a supernatural manner.

barge.description: A flat-bottomed boat used for transporting people or goods, often on rivers.

chapkan.description: A traditional Indian long coat or tunic, often worn as outerwear.

pajamas.description: Loose-fitting trousers, traditionally worn in South Asia as nightwear or casual attire.

waistband.description: A cloth belt or sash tied around the waist, often used to secure clothing or carry small items.

turban.description: A long piece of cloth wound around the head, commonly worn in South Asia as a traditional headdress.

sal tree.description: A large, deciduous tree native to the Indian subcontinent, valued for its hardwood.

RamBholi.description: A woman from Nanak's neighborhood, previously mute, who is revealed to be of high status and plays a key role in the unfolding events.

Harihar.description: A person mentioned as about to arrive, possibly an authority figure or enforcer among the women.

bajra.description: A specific barge or boat referenced in the story, possibly with magical or narrative significance.

munj.description: A type of tough grass (Saccharum munja) used for making ropes and mats in India.

loincloth.description: A simple garment worn around the waist, often by ascetics or laborers in India.

sacred thread.description: A symbolic thread worn by Hindu men after a coming-of-age ritual, signifying their initiation into spiritual life.

lotus posture.description: A cross-legged sitting position (padmasana) used in meditation and yoga.

deerskin.description: A traditional mat made from the hide of a deer, often used by ascetics for meditation.

conch.description: A large seashell (shankha) used as a ceremonial horn in Hindu rituals.

chobdars.description: Palace attendants or doorkeepers, often distinguished by carrying staffs.

Dhanpati.description: A woman with a significant role in the plot, previously escaped with Rambholi from Nanak; her name and identity are noted as mysterious and important.

Pandit Jagannath Jyotishi.description: A learned man and ally of the protagonists, who is present in disguise as the Daroga (warden) and attempts to help Kunwar Anand Singh.

Mathuraji.description: A place referenced as Lali's home, likely referring to the city of Mathura, an ancient and culturally significant city in India.

barvai.description: A specific form of Hindi verse or poetic riddle, often used to convey secret messages.

Sahib.description: A term of respect or honorific, often used after a title or name.

Diwan Ramanand.description: Diwan Ramanand is a high-ranking minister or administrator, involved in the affairs of Rohtasgarh.

Shersingh.description: Shersingh is a renowned aiyyar, Kamla's uncle, formerly in Digvijay Singh's service, later joins Virendra Singh's side.

Gadādharsingh.description: Gadādharsingh is Shersingh's younger brother and Kamla's father, deceased by the time of this chapter.

Randhirsingh.description: Randhirsingh is a former friend of Digvijay Singh, grandfather of Kishori.

Raja Virendrasingh.description: Another form of addressing King Virendra Singh, emphasizing his royal status.

tribute.description: A payment or revenue imposed by a superior ruler on a subordinate kingdom as a sign of allegiance.

deputy.description: A person appointed to act as a ruler or administrator in place of the king.

committee.description: A group of select individuals convened to discuss and decide important matters.

masked man.description: A person whose identity is concealed, often for secrecy or dramatic revelation.

folding his hands.description: A gesture of respect or supplication in Indian culture, often performed before superiors.

Maharaj Digvijay Singh.description: The king of Rohtasgarh, involved in the events surrounding the underground vault and the sacrifices before the terrifying idol.

Rama.description: One of Kundan's loyal followers who assists in the escape of Kishori from the cave.

barwa.description: A type of poetic or coded message, referenced here as something written by Dhanpati in the underground chamber.

bundle.description: A small package or cloth-wrapped parcel, commonly used for carrying personal items or tools in Indian settings.

Agnidev.description: The Hindu god of fire, invoked by Kishori as she faces death.

pyre.description: A pile of wood used for burning a body as part of a funeral or execution.

Kunwar Indrajit Singh.description: The elder son of Raja Virendra Singh and Chandrakanta, a brave and handsome prince (Kunwar). He is the central hero of the story, skilled in warfare and deeply in love with Kishori.

Raja Virendra Singh.description: Son of Surendra Singh and King of Chunar. Husband of Chandrakanta, father of Indrajit Singh and Anand Singh. A just and powerful ruler waging war against Shivdutt.
